recently_processed.title: New software package: ERPLAB Studio
recently_processed.content:
We are excited to announce the release of a new EEG/ERP analysis package, ERPLAB Studio. We think it’s a huge improvement over the classic EEGLAB user interface. See our cheesy “advertisement” video to get a quick overview.

Rather than operating as an EEGLAB plugin, ERPLAB Studio is a standalone Matlab program that provides a more efficient and user-friendly interface to the most commonly used EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines.

With ERPLAB Studio, you automatically see the EEG or ERP waveforms as soon as you load a file. And as soon as you perform an operation, you see what the new EEG/ERP looks like. For example, when you filter the data, you immediately see the filtered waveforms.

You can even select multiple datasets and apply an operation like artifact detection on all of them in one step. And then you can immediately see the results, such as which EEG epochs have been marked with artifacts.

We give you access to EEGLAB’s ICA-based artifact correction tools, but with a nice bonus. You can plot the ICA activations in the same window with the EEG data, making it easy to see which ICA components correspond to specific artifacts such as eyeblinks.

The program has an EEG tab for processing continuous and epoched EEG data, and an ERP tab for processing averaged ERPs.

The automatic ERP plotting makes it easy for you to view the data laid out according to the electrode locations. And we have an Advanced Waveform Viewer that can make publication-quality plots.

ERPLAB Studio is mainly just a new user interface. Under the hood, we’re running the same EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines you’ve always used. And scripting is identical.

ERPLAB Studio is included in version 11 and higher of ERPLAB. You simply follow our download/installation instructions and then type estudio from the Matlab command line.

If you’re new to ERPLAB, we strongly recommend that you go through our tutorial before starting to process your own data.

If you already know how to use the original version of ERPLAB (which we now call ERPLAB Classic), you can quickly learn how to use ERPLAB Studio with our Transition Guide.

We also have a manual that describes every feature in detail.

recently_processed.title: A preclinical platform for focused ultrasound delivery from microplate to awake brain
recently_processed.content: Background. Focused ultrasound (FUS) has broad therapeutic potential, but its mechanisms of action are poorly understood. Preclinical FUS research enables rigorous interrogation of understudied parameters, but fragmented, single-purpose benchtop devices prevent standardized acoustic exposure across models. Objective. To describe a unified preclinical FUS platform for cell culture, ex vivo tissue, and awake stereotaxic in vivo delivery in one lightweight system, validated using glioblastoma as a disease model. Methods. We performed single-well FUS delivery to 96-well microplates, single-well delivery to freshly resected human glioblastoma tissue, and stereotaxic transcranial delivery to awake, head-fixed mice ambulating freely on a floating cage. Output was independently calibrated in free field, with measured microplate insertion loss. Pulsed low-intensity focused ultrasound (pLIFU) was applied to GL261-bearing mice, resected human glioblastoma, and macrophage cell lines. Results. Awake stereotaxic pLIFU produced acute tumor signal attenuation in GL261-bearing mice (mean log2 fold-change -1.66 versus +5.20 controls, p = 0.016) with bioluminescence evidence consistent with focal targeting. Ex vivo pLIFU produced directionally consistent immunophenotypic shifts in human glioblastoma (increased iNOS+, decreased Arg1+ populations). In vitro, pLIFU reduced CD80 on immunosuppressive macrophages to 73% of baseline in RAW 264.7 cells (p = 0.0008, n = 5) and 64% in THP-1 cells (p = 0.0006, n = 2), with MHC II upregulation in RAW 264.7 (ratio 1.65, p = 0.004) and ARG1 reduction in THP-1 (ratio 0.52, p = 0.0025). Conclusions. A unified preclinical FUS platform validated across in vitro, ex vivo, and awake in vivo applications enables stereotaxically guided transcranial FUS in awake, head-fixed mice ambulating in an exploratory manner during sonication, and single-well microplate treatments.

recently_processed.title: Individualized brain-body signatures of positive emotions revealed by large-scale multimodal neurophysiological recording
recently_processed.content: Using one of the most comprehensive multimodal biosensing datasets in affective research, densely sampled within individuals, we asked how emotions are instantiated in each person's brain and body. Four participants viewed 168 emotion-evoking videos during 128-channel EEG and 28 autonomic, ocular and facial recordings. Cross-validated elastic-net classifiers distinguished each of 15 positive and neutral emotions from baseline in every participant (mean accuracy 87-97%). We found that no emotion was predicted by a single marker and each reflected a multimodal ensemble of cortical and autonomic activity whose composition was largely person-specific. Yet physiology-derived groupings converged selectively with self-report; Interest-Awe-Amusement-Satisfaction and Entrancement-Aesthetic Appreciation recurred across individuals based on physiology. Across emotion groups, frontal and posterior delta, posterior alpha and electrodermal activity formed a shared backbone, plausibly reflecting affective and sensory engagement, whereas cardiovascular and facial signals varied between people. This framework yields individualized, objective neurophysiological indicators of emotion, potentially aiding personalized diagnosis.

recently_processed.title: Executive and language systems competitively shape predictive processing during reading
recently_processed.content: When we read, our brains constantly generate predictions about upcoming words, which is thought to make comprehension faster and more efficient. Yet it remains unclear whether this predictive mechanism relies on the same domain-general executive resources the brain uses for other demanding cognitive tasks, or operates largely independently within the language system. Here we tested this question using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in twenty-five healthy adults, who performed self-paced naturalistic reading, an n-back task, and a dual task of concurrent reading and n-back, allowing us to place competing demands on cognitive resources. In three sessions, we stimulated the left angular gyrus alone, the angular gyrus together with dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a hub of executive control, or delivered sham stimulation, and used computational modeling of decision-making to isolate how each brain state altered the underlying cognitive processes. Combined stimulation of the angular gyrus and prefrontal cortex selectively weakened the reading-time costs of unexpected words, but only when reading competed with the working-memory task, revealing that linguistic prediction draws on executive resources specifically under cognitive load. Computational models showed that the relationship was bidirectional: Unpredictable words also disrupted concurrent working-memory decisions, slowing the accumulation of evidence and increasing response caution. Together, these findings show that predictive language processing is not a fixed, encapsulated function but is dynamically coupled to executive control when cognitive demands compete. Our results provide evidence that prediction during language comprehension is embedded within a broader, demand-sensitive cognitive architecture that flexibly coordinates linguistic and executive resources.

recently_processed.title: Anatomical Connectivity of the Macaque Gaze-following Patch
recently_processed.content: The macaque gaze-following patch (GFP) is a specialized region of the temporal cortex implicated in decoding others' focus of attention and guiding gaze-following behavior. Although the GFP has been characterized functionally, its anatomical connectivity remains largely unknown. To investigate how the GFP is embedded within a putative brain network supporting social interactions, we injected a pair of fluorescence labeled anterograde and retrograde tracers into the GFP of one monkey. Analysis of the resulting material revealed reciprocal connections between the GFP and a region of the inferior parietal lobule, likely corresponding to area PFG, as well as sparse retrograde labeling in the amygdala. In contrast to the expectation that the GFP might be subject to cognitive control signals from the prefrontal cortex, we failed to identify convincing retrograde labeling in prefrontal regions. Overall, this connectivity profile is consistent with a network that translates information derived from others' faces into shifts of attention, while providing little evidence for direct prefrontal control of the GFP.

recently_processed.title: Affective representations and brain-body dynamics during emotional video viewing
recently_processed.content: Emotional events evoke changing neural and bodily responses, but how these responses relate to overall emotional evaluations and how brain and body responses correspond over time remain unclear. Ninety-two participants viewed 25 silent emotional videos, each approximately one minute long, and rated valence and arousal after each video. We recorded brain activity using magnetoencephalography alongside cardiac, electrodermal, respiratory and facial-muscle activity. Representational similarity analysis (RSA) compared source-resolved cortical spectral patterns and peripheral response patterns with participants' valence and arousal ratings, adjusting each affective dimension for the other. Across whole videos, valence similarity corresponded to beta-band power patterns predominantly in left sensorimotor and frontotemporal cortex and to facial-muscle responses. Arousal similarity corresponded to alpha-band power patterns in the right frontoparietal cortex and to phasic electrodermal activity. The neural associations persisted after adjustment for visual and semantic similarities between the videos. Windowed neural correspondence with retrospective valence was significant from around 10 s onwards, with both neural and facial-muscle associations strengthening towards the end of the videos, whereas no significant windowed arousal associations were detected throughout viewing. We further applied dynamic RSA to compare neural and physiological response patterns across videos at different temporal lags. Correspondence exceeded a temporally decoupled reference for facial muscles, heart rate and electrodermal activity, but not respiration rate. On average, corrugator activity preceded corresponding neural patterns by about 1 s, zygomaticus activity occurred at approximately the same time, and heart-rate and electrodermal activity followed about 1.7 s and 4.5 s later, respectively. Together, these findings link overall affective evaluations to complementary neural and peripheral response geometries and reveal signal-specific temporal profiles of ongoing brain-body correspondence.
